segments.en: Akwaaba! You will hear that word the moment you arrive. In the Twi language it means welcome, and in Ghana it is said with a big smile and often a handshake that ends in a friendly finger snap.

Ghana sits on the Gulf of Guinea in West Africa, close to where the equator meets the prime meridian. Palm-lined beaches run along the south, forests cover the middle, and the north opens into wide, dry savanna.

In 1957, Ghana became one of the first African countries south of the Sahara to win independence. Its leader, Kwame Nkrumah, declared that Ghana was free forever, and the black star on the flag still shines for that moment.
Accra, the capital, is loud, lively and full of colour. Tro-tros, the shared minibuses, weave through traffic, and at Makola Market you can buy anything from yams to fabric to hair beads.
About that fabric. Kente cloth, woven by the Asante and Ewe peoples, is made of narrow strips of brilliant thread sewn together. Every colour and pattern has a meaning.

In the city of Kumasi lies the heart of the Asante kingdom, with its king, the Asantehene. The Golden Stool, which Asante people believe holds the soul of their nation, is so sacred that no one may sit on it.
Along the coast, whitewashed castles such as Cape Coast and Elmina tell a painful story of the Atlantic slave trade. Many visitors, including descendants of those taken, come to remember and reflect.

Now, the food. Jollof rice, cooked in a spicy tomato sauce, is a matter of national pride, and a friendly rivalry with Nigeria over whose is best. Try fufu too, pounded cassava and plantain dipped into light soup or groundnut soup.
Kelewele is a favourite snack: ripe plantain cubes spiced with ginger and pepper and fried until golden. And much of the world's chocolate begins with cocoa grown on small farms in Ghana's forests.
Music is everywhere. Highlife blends guitars and horns into dancing rhythms, and the newer sounds of hiplife and Afrobeats pour out of radios and phone speakers on every street.
A little etiquette: use your right hand to greet, give or eat. Many Ghanaians also carry a day name for the day they were born, like Kofi for a boy born on a Friday.
Before you go, cheer on the Black Stars, the national football team, with the whole country. Then head west to Côte d'Ivoire, or east to Togo, both just along the coast.
